articles.title: Understanding ANSI/BHMA Lock Grades: A Guide for Your Customers
articles.author: Patricia Morales
articles.summary: A clear breakdown of ANSI/BHMA Grade 1, 2, and 3 lock ratings to help locksmiths and security professionals advise their customers on the right level of protection.
articles.body:
One of the most common questions locksmiths hear is: what grade lock do I need? Here is a quick reference you can share with your customers or use to guide product selection.

Grade 3 is the baseline residential standard. These locks pass 200,000 cycle tests and provide adequate security for interior doors and low-risk residential entries. Most builder-grade hardware falls into this category.

Grade 2 offers enhanced durability and security. With 400,000 cycle testing and higher forced-entry resistance, Grade 2 locks are appropriate for residential exterior doors, light commercial applications, and multi-family common areas.

Grade 1 is the highest ANSI/BHMA rating. These locks withstand 800,000 cycles and meet stringent forced-entry criteria. Grade 1 hardware is required by most commercial building codes and is the standard for schools, hospitals, government facilities, and any high-traffic opening.

At Keystone, we stock all three grades across our residential and commercial lock lines. If you are specifying hardware for a project and need help matching the right grade to the application, our technical support team is available to review door schedules and recommend products.

articles.title: Five Tips for Faster Transponder Key Programming
articles.author: Patricia Morales
articles.summary: Practical advice for automotive locksmiths looking to improve efficiency and reduce callbacks on transponder key programming jobs.
articles.body:
Transponder programming is one of the fastest-growing revenue streams for locksmith shops. Here are five tips from our technical support team to help you complete jobs faster and avoid common pitfalls.

1. Update your programmer firmware before heading to a job site. Manufacturers like Autel release vehicle coverage updates monthly. An outdated database is the most common cause of failed programming attempts.

2. Verify the key blank part number against the vehicle VIN, not just the make and model. Year-to-year changes in immobilizer systems can mean a different blank even for the same model.

3. Keep a charged backup battery pack for your programmer. Low battery warnings mid-procedure can interrupt communication with the vehicle ECU and require starting the process over.

4. For all-keys-lost situations, confirm the procedure steps before starting. Some vehicles require a specific sequence of ignition cycles or a timed waiting period. Knowing the process in advance avoids frustration on site.

5. Stock the top 20 transponder blanks on your van. Based on our sales data, Toyota, Honda, Ford, GM, and Nissan blanks account for over 70% of transponder key jobs in our territory. Carrying these blanks means fewer trips back to the shop or waiting for delivery.

Keystone stocks transponder blanks from Ilco, JMA USA, and Strattec, along with Autel and Xtool programming equipment. Contact us if you need help building your automotive key inventory.

articles.title: Keystone Marks 37 Years of Service to Mid-Atlantic Security Professionals
articles.author: Michael Hartwell
articles.summary: Keystone Security Distribution celebrates 37 years in business, reflecting on growth from a single-person warehouse to a 42-employee regional distributor serving six states.
articles.body:
This month marks 37 years since my father, Bob Hartwell, opened the doors of Keystone Security Distribution in a rented warehouse space in King of Prussia, Pennsylvania. What started as a one-person operation serving a handful of locksmith shops in southeastern PA has grown into a 42-employee company with two warehouse locations and over 150 active customer accounts across six states and the District of Columbia.

A few milestones worth noting: our annual revenue has grown to nearly $20 million, we maintain over 8,500 SKUs in stock with a 97.3% same-day ship rate, and we have expanded our product expertise from traditional locks and keys into access control, automotive key programming, and safe distribution.

But the numbers only tell part of the story. What has not changed in 37 years is the way we do business. We answer the phone. We know our customers by name. We stand behind what we sell. Those principles were not a business strategy; they are just how my father believed a company should operate, and we intend to keep it that way.

Thank you to our customers, our manufacturer partners, and our team members who make Keystone what it is. Here is to the next 37.

articles.title: Access Control Trends to Watch: Mobile Credentials, Cloud Platforms, and PoE Locks
articles.author: Patricia Morales
articles.summary: An overview of three access control trends shaping the market and how security integrators can position themselves for growth.
articles.body:
The access control market is evolving rapidly, and integrators who stay ahead of these trends will be well-positioned for growth in the coming years.

Mobile Credentials: Smartphone-based access is moving from early adoption to mainstream demand. Building owners and property managers are asking for cardless entry, and the technology has matured to the point where it is reliable and cost-effective. HID Mobile Access and other platforms make it possible to issue, revoke, and manage credentials remotely.

Cloud-Managed Access Control: Traditional on-premises access control servers are giving way to cloud-hosted platforms that reduce IT overhead and enable remote management. For integrators, this shift changes the sales conversation from a capital expenditure to a recurring service model.

PoE-Powered Locks: Power over Ethernet locks eliminate the need for separate power supplies and reduce installation labor. As building network infrastructure improves, PoE locks offer a cleaner, faster installation path, especially in retrofit scenarios.

Keystone stocks the hardware to support all three trends, from HID multi-technology readers and controllers to PoE-enabled access panels. Our technical team can help you design systems that incorporate these technologies. Reach out to discuss your next project.

articles.title: Master Keying Best Practices: Planning a System That Scales
articles.author: Patricia Morales
articles.summary: Guidelines for designing master key systems that are secure, organized, and expandable, avoiding common mistakes that create problems down the road.
articles.body:
A well-designed master key system provides convenience and security. A poorly designed one creates headaches for years. Here are best practices from our technical support team.

Start with a key schedule. Before pinning a single cylinder, map out the hierarchy: grand master, master, sub-master, and change key levels. Document every door, every key holder, and every access level. This upfront planning prevents conflicts and cross-keying problems later.

Use a restricted keyway when security matters. Standard keyways like SC1 and KW1 can be duplicated at any hardware store. For facilities that need key control, specify a restricted keyway such as Schlage Primus or Corbin Russwin Pyramid. Blanks are available only through authorized channels, which means you control who gets copies.

Leave room for expansion. A system designed for exactly the number of doors you have today will run out of usable combinations when the building adds a wing or a new tenant moves in. Build in at least 25 percent capacity above current needs.

Document everything. Maintain a key records binder or digital file for each system you install. Include the key schedule, pinning chart, key blank part numbers, and a contact log. When the customer calls five years later for additional keys, you will have everything you need.

Keystone stocks pinning kits, key blanks, and restricted keyway cylinders for Schlage, Kwikset, Corbin Russwin, and Best. Our technical team can review your key schedule and verify pinning combinations before you start the job.

articles.title: Safe Selection Guide: Matching Fire and Burglary Ratings to Customer Needs
articles.author: James Kowalski
articles.summary: A practical guide to UL fire and burglary ratings for safes, helping locksmiths and dealers recommend the right protection level for residential and commercial applications.
articles.body:
When a customer asks for a safe, the first question should not be about size or price. It should be about what they are protecting and from what threat. Here is a quick guide to the ratings that matter.

Fire Ratings: UL fire ratings indicate how long a safe protects its contents at a specified temperature. Common ratings include 30 minutes at 1,550 degrees F, one hour at 1,700 degrees F, and two hours at 1,850 degrees F. For important documents, recommend at least a one-hour rating. For irreplaceable items or media storage, two hours provides an additional safety margin.

Burglary Ratings: UL burglary ratings reflect resistance to physical attack. B-Rate safes have a steel body of at least 1/2 inch with a combination or electronic lock. TL-15 safes resist attack with common hand and electric tools for 15 minutes. TL-30 provides 30 minutes of resistance. For retail cash handling, B-Rate deposit safes are standard. For jewelry, pharmaceuticals, or high-value inventory, TL-15 or TL-30 is appropriate.

Residential Recommendations: Home safes with a one-hour fire rating and electronic keypad lock cover most residential needs. For firearm storage, recommend a dedicated gun safe with a fire rating and pry-resistant door construction.

Commercial Recommendations: Match the burglary rating to the contents. Cash-handling businesses need at minimum a B-Rate deposit safe. High-value commercial operations should consider TL-15 or TL-30 depending on insurance requirements.

Keystone stocks safes from Liberty Safe, AMSEC, Hollon, and Gardall in fire-rated, burglary-rated, and combination configurations. Contact us for project pricing on multi-unit orders.
